questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — a CRUD product end-to-end in 45 minutes [mid] (jsprojectlearn, content/modules/system-design-for-crud.md). Scenario: an appointment-booking web app for a chain of clinics. About 1M daily users make roughly 20 requests each; clinic staff publish time slots, patients search, book, cancel and reschedule, and a slot may be held by exactly one patient. Every clinic's data must stay private to that clinic, and patients get a confirmation email. Run the interview script out loud before you look: requirements, rough numbers, API, data model with keys and indexes, one read path and one write path, the scaling moves, the failure modes, and what you would defer. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Opens with requirements, both lists: functional (book, cancel, reschedule, search slots) and non-functional (how many, how fast, how correct), and asks which wins when they conflict, consistency or availability; for slot booking a defensible answer is consistency, since two patients must never hold one slot.
keyPoints.quote: Ask which matters more when they conflict

keyPoints.text: [w2] Rough numbers with a day rounded to 100,000 seconds: 1M users x 20 requests is about 200 requests a second on average, planned at roughly 5x for the peak.
keyPoints.quote: Round a day to 100,000 seconds.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Draws the conclusion the numbers allow and says it out loud: a single well-indexed Postgres primary carries this load and storage with room to spare, so no sharding or exotic store.
keyPoints.quote: Most systems in these rounds fit on one primary database with room to spare, and saying so is the correct answer.

keyPoints.text: [w2] A small REST surface of five or six endpoints (list slots, create booking, cancel, reschedule, my bookings), with list endpoints taking a cursor and a limit rather than page numbers.
keyPoints.quote: Five or six endpoints, in the style of the

keyPoints.text: [w3] The data model puts the one-slot-one-patient rule in the database: a unique index on (resource_id, slot_start) (a partial unique index such as WHERE status = 'active' also counts, so a cancelled booking frees the slot), or an exclusion constraint when bookings are overlapping time ranges, so the second concurrent insert fails and the API answers 409.
keyPoints.quote: The loser's insert fails, and you return 409.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Walks one read request and one write request through the system end to end, naming the indexes each query uses.
keyPoints.quote: Walk one request of each through the system.

keyPoints.text: [w2] The confirmation email is a job enqueued after the booking transaction commits, never sent inside the request.
keyPoints.quote: a job on a queue after the transaction commits

keyPoints.text: [w1] Closes the 45 minutes with what was deliberately deferred and what would be built next.
keyPoints.quote: What you deferred, and what you would build next

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same booking app at 10x: about 2,000 requests a second on average with a lunchtime peak several times higher, the primary database pinned on CPU, and, since an earlier quick fix moved most reads onto read replicas, patients reporting that a booking they just made is missing from "My appointments". What breaks first, which move do you make first, and what in your design already handles it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The first move is the cheapest one: find the slow queries, EXPLAIN them, add the missing index and remove the N+1, because that fixes most real database-bottleneck incidents before any new infrastructure.
keyPoints.quote: add the missing index, kill the N+1

keyPoints.text: [w2] Second: cache only the hot reads that tolerate staleness (the public slot list, not the booking itself) and put static assets and media on a CDN.
keyPoints.quote: put static assets and media on a CDN

keyPoints.text: [w2] Third: run several stateless app instances behind a load balancer, which requires sessions and uploaded files to live outside the process.
keyPoints.quote: sessions and files move out of the process

keyPoints.text: [w3] The missing booking is replication lag from read replicas: the write went to the primary and the next read hit a lagging replica. Fix read-your-writes by routing that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write, or always reading their own data from it.
keyPoints.quote: sending a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write

keyPoints.text: [w2] Slow or spiky work (emails, reminders, exports) moves onto a queue so the request returns quickly and a worker catches up.
keyPoints.quote: so a request returns quickly and a worker catches up

keyPoints.text: [w3] The double-booking race stays correct under load at 10x, because two requests can both pass an application-level check but the database constraint serialises them; no lock in app code is needed.
keyPoints.quote: constraint is the only thing that serialises them, so that is where the rule

keyPoints.text: [w1] Partitioning or splitting out a service comes only after all of the above, and only if the numbers still demand it.
keyPoints.quote: Only then: partitioning, or splitting out a service.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your booking design against the alternatives the guide names: how clinics are separated and how that is enforced, how concurrent edits and counters are handled, and the things you chose not to build yet: microservices, Kafka or another event bus, a cache added before measuring, and a dedicated search engine. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Tenancy: shared tables with a tenant_id on every row is the cheapest and usual answer; a schema per tenant or a database per tenant buys stronger isolation at the price of the most operational work.
keyPoints.quote: shared tables with a `tenant_id` on every row

keyPoints.text: [w3] The tenancy rule is enforced below the handlers, with Postgres row-level security or an EF Core global query filter, so a single forgotten WHERE clause cannot expose another clinic's patients.
keyPoints.quote: one forgotten `WHERE` cannot leak data

keyPoints.text: [w2] Reschedules and edits guard against lost updates with an optimistic version column, answering 409 when the version no longer matches.
keyPoints.quote: an optimistic `version` column, 409 on mismatch

keyPoints.text: [w2] Capacity counters are decremented with a conditional UPDATE (WHERE remaining > 0) and the affected row count is checked; never read the value, subtract in code and write it back.
keyPoints.quote: Never read, subtract and write back.

keyPoints.text: [w2] One deployable rather than microservices, until a team or scaling boundary forces a split.
keyPoints.quote: One deployable until a team or scaling boundary forces a

keyPoints.text: [w2] A database-backed queue instead of Kafka, since it already handles thousands of jobs a second.
keyPoints.quote: A database-backed queue handles thousands of jobs per second.

keyPoints.text: [w2] No cache before measuring: it adds invalidation bugs to a system that may not need it.
keyPoints.quote: It adds invalidation bugs to a system that may

keyPoints.text: [w1] Slot and clinic search starts with Postgres full-text search; a dedicated search engine, fed from a queue, only when relevance or scale demands it.
keyPoints.quote: only when relevance or scale demands it, fed from a queue
